prompt: A program sends `GET /ana-uploads/photos/2026/cat.jpg` over HTTPS and gets the whole file back. What kind of storage is it talking to?
hint: Look at how the data is addressed.

choices.text: A file share mounted over NFS
choices.why: An NFS share is reached by mounting it and opening a path, not by an HTTP request.

choices.text: A block volume attached to the instance
choices.why: A volume answers block reads from the operating system; nothing on it speaks HTTP.

choices.text: An object store reached over HTTP
choices.why: Right. A key in a bucket, requested whole over HTTP, is what an object store is.

choices.text: A local disk formatted with ext4
choices.why: A local filesystem is read through system calls on a path, never through `GET`.

prompt: Match each kind of storage to what a piece of data in it is addressed by.
hint: One kind of address per kind of storage.

pairs.right: A block number on one volume
A path in a shared filesystem

right_distractors: An IP address and a port

prompt: On a block volume, what decides that blocks 2048 to 2055 hold part of `/var/log/syslog`?
hint: Who formatted the volume?

choices.text: The storage service, which tracks every file on each volume
choices.why: The service only knows numbered blocks; it has no idea what file they belong to.

choices.text: The filesystem of the instance's operating system
choices.why: Right. The operating system formatted the volume and keeps the map from files to blocks.

choices.text: The hypervisor
choices.why: The hypervisor passes blocks through to the instance and reads no filesystem.

choices.text: Nothing: a volume keeps whole files
choices.why: That describes an object store more than a volume, and even there a key is not a path on a disk.

prompt: A 2 GB log must be extended one line at a time by a single process, without rewriting what is already there. Where can that process do it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which interfaces let a program write into an existing file?

choices.text: On a block volume the instance has mounted
choices.why: Yes. The filesystem on the volume supports appending, like any local disk.

choices.text: As an object in S3 Standard
choices.why: No. An object is replaced whole; a longer log is a new object, written from the start.

choices.text: On a managed file share mounted over NFS
choices.why: Yes. A network filesystem allows appending, at the cost of a round trip per write.

choices.text: As an object in Glacier Instant Retrieval
choices.why: No. The class changes the price, not the interface: it is still written whole.

prompt: What does a 200 GB `gp3` volume cost for one month in `sa-east-1`, at the sheet's price of 0.1520 USD per GB-month?
hint: Size times price; the fill level does not enter.

prompt: An instance runs in zone A. The volume it needs was created in zone B of the same region. What has to happen?
hint: Where does a volume live?

choices.text: Attach it anyway; the traffic crosses zones and is slower
choices.why: A volume cannot be attached across zones at all; it is not a matter of speed.

choices.text: Attach it read-only, which is allowed between zones
choices.why: There is no read-only exception; the zone is where the volume exists.

choices.text: Snapshot it and create a new volume from the snapshot in zone A
choices.why: Right. A volume lives in one zone, and a snapshot is how its data moves to another.

choices.text: Detach it; a detached volume moves to wherever it is needed
choices.why: Detaching changes which instance holds it, never which zone it is in.

prompt: A 500 GB `gp3` volume holds 40 GB of files. What is the monthly bill for it based on?
hint: When is the size chosen?

choices.text: The 40 GB actually written
choices.why: That is how EFS and S3 bill. A volume bills what was provisioned.

choices.text: The 500 GB provisioned when it was created
choices.why: Right. The meter runs on the size chosen at creation, full or empty.

choices.text: The hours the instance using it was running
choices.why: A volume bills while it exists, attached or not; a stopped instance does not stop it.

choices.text: The number of reads and writes
choices.why: Baseline IOPS come with a `gp3` volume; the bill line is its size.

prompt: A database on a 500 GB `gp3` volume is slow, and the volume is doing its full baseline of 3,000 IOPS of small scattered reads all day. What is the cheapest change that addresses the cause?
hint: Which dial is at its limit?

choices.text: Buy more IOPS on the same volume, without adding gigabytes
choices.why: Right. `gp3` sells IOPS separately from size, and IOPS are what run out.

choices.text: Move the data to `st1`, which is cheaper per GB
choices.why: `st1` is built for long sequential reads and is slow at scattered ones: it would make this worse.

choices.text: Grow the volume to 2 TB so that it gets faster
choices.why: That was the habit on older types. On `gp3` size and IOPS are separate, so the space buys nothing here.

choices.text: Attach the volume to a second instance to share the load
choices.why: A volume is attached to one instance at a time, and a second reader would not raise its IOPS.

prompt: The number of separate small reads or writes a volume performs each second is measured in ___.
hint: Four letters, the dial `gp3` sells apart from size.

prompt: You restore last Tuesday's snapshot of a volume. What do you get?
hint: Does anything happen to the existing volume?

choices.text: The existing volume, rewound to Tuesday
choices.why: Restoring never touches the existing volume.

choices.text: Tuesday's files copied into the running filesystem
choices.why: A snapshot holds blocks, not files, and it is not merged into anything.

choices.text: A new volume with Tuesday's contents
choices.why: Right. You create a volume from the snapshot, in the zone you choose, and attach it.

choices.text: A download of Tuesday's blocks from a bucket of yours
choices.why: Snapshots sit in the provider's object storage, not in any bucket you can open.

prompt: A volume holds 60 GB of data and 2 GB change each day. After a month of daily snapshots, the first full and 29 incremental, what do the snapshots cost for that month in `sa-east-1`, at 0.0680 USD per GB-month?
hint: Add up what the snapshots hold, then multiply.

prompt: An attacker holding an administrator's keys to a company's only account deletes its volumes and all their snapshots, everything in `sa-east-1`. Which arrangement would have left a copy to restore?
hint: What could those credentials not reach?

choices.text: Snapshots every hour instead of every day
choices.why: More snapshots in the same account are deleted by the same credentials.

choices.text: Copies kept in a second account
choices.why: Right. A backup policy keeps one copy beyond the reach of the production account.

choices.text: Snapshots stored in a second zone of the region
choices.why: Snapshots already outlive a zone; the problem is who can delete them, not where they are.

choices.text: Nothing: eleven nines of durability covers it
choices.why: Durability is about hardware failing. A delete request is carried out faithfully.

prompt: Three web servers must write uploaded files into the same `uploads` directory, and the application cannot be changed. What fits?
hint: The application wants a path, on several machines at once.

choices.text: A managed file share mounted on all three
choices.why: Right. A shared filesystem is exactly a path several machines write at once.

choices.text: One `gp3` volume attached to all three servers
choices.why: A volume attaches to one instance, and three kernels writing one ext4 would corrupt it.

choices.text: A bucket, with each server using its own key
choices.why: A bucket would be cheaper, but it needs the code change the question rules out.

choices.text: A volume per server, synchronised by snapshots
choices.why: Snapshots make new volumes; they never keep three running ones in step.

prompt: A build that runs `npm install` takes 40 seconds on a local volume and several minutes when the project sits on an NFS file share. What explains most of it?
hint: Count the files, then count what each one costs.

choices.text: The share throttles package managers
choices.why: Nothing on a file share knows which program is asking.

choices.text: Thousands of small files, each operation a network round trip
choices.why: Right. Per file, a network filesystem pays a round trip that a local disk does not.

choices.text: The share has to grow before each new file is written
choices.why: It grows with what is stored, in the background; nobody waits for it.

choices.text: NFS always stores data on hard disks
choices.why: NFS is a protocol and says nothing about the media behind it.

prompt: What does keeping 500 GB in S3 Standard for one month cost in `sa-east-1`, at 0.04050 USD per GB-month?
hint: Gigabytes times price.

prompt: An EFS Standard filesystem in `sa-east-1` holds 40 GB for a month. At 0.5700 USD per GB-month, what does it cost?
hint: EFS bills what is stored.

prompt: Put these sheet lines in order of price per GB-month in `sa-east-1`, cheapest first.
hint: Object, then block, then file; the cold class sits below them all.
trap: EFS below a volume is the usual slip: per gigabyte stored, the shared filesystem is the dearest line on the sheet.

prompt: An application uploads one million objects to S3 in `sa-east-1` in a month. At 0.00700 USD per 1,000 `PUT` requests, what do the requests alone cost?
hint: How many thousands are in a million?

prompt: A team compares 500 GB of EFS (285.00 a month) with a 500 GB `gp3` volume (76.00) and concludes the file share costs nearly four times as much. The data will be 60 GB. What does the comparison miss?
hint: Which of the two bills what is stored?

choices.text: EFS adds a charge per instance that mounts the filesystem
choices.why: Mounts are not a line on the sheet; the storage line is what matters here.

choices.text: The volume would also bill each read
choices.why: `gp3` includes its baseline IOPS; reads are not billed one by one.

choices.text: Nothing; the ratio holds at any size
choices.why: It holds only when both are full. One bills stored data, the other provisioned size.

choices.text: EFS bills the 60 GB stored, 34.20, less than the volume
choices.why: Right. 60 × 0.5700 = 34.20, while the volume bills its 500 GB whatever it holds.

prompt: In the key `photos/2026/cat.jpg`, the beginning `photos/` is not a folder but a ___ that a listing can group keys by.
hint: The word the console hides behind a folder icon.

prompt: In an object store, what does renaming `reports/q3.txt` to `reports/2026-q3.txt` actually take?
hint: Where is the name kept?

choices.text: One rename request that changes the name in place
choices.why: There is no rename request: the key is the object's only name.

choices.text: A copy to the new key and a delete of the old one
choices.why: Right. Two requests at least, and for a moment both keys exist.

choices.text: Moving the object into the `2026-q3` folder
choices.why: There are no folders to move into, only keys that share a beginning.

choices.text: Nothing, since keys are only labels in the console
choices.why: The key is how every request finds the object; changing it is the whole job.

prompt: A program keeps its log as one object in a bucket and has to add one line to it. What does it do?
hint: Can part of an object be written?

choices.text: Sends a `PUT` with an append flag
choices.why: There is no append in the interface; a `PUT` always writes the whole object.

choices.text: Opens the object in append mode through the SDK
choices.why: An SDK wraps the same HTTP requests, and none of them opens an object.

choices.text: Writes a byte range at the end with a ranged `PUT`
choices.why: Ranges work for reading with `GET`; writing part of an object is not possible.

choices.text: Rewrites the whole object with the line added
choices.why: Right. An object is replaced whole; the new one simply has one more line.

prompt: One program's `PUT` to a key in S3 has just returned success. A second program immediately sends a `GET` for the same key. What does it receive?
hint: What changed in December 2020?

choices.text: Possibly the old version, for a few seconds
choices.why: That was the behaviour of overwrites before December 2020.

choices.text: A 404 until the object reaches every zone
choices.why: The success is returned after the object is stored; a read then finds it.

choices.text: The new object, every time
choices.why: Right. S3 is strongly consistent for reads after writes.

choices.text: Whatever a `LIST` has shown so far
choices.why: A `GET` by key does not go through a listing, and a listing is consistent too.

prompt: Match each request to what it does to `/bucket/key`.
hint: Five verbs of HTTP, four in use.

pairs.right: Stores a whole object, replacing any already there
Returns the object, or a byte range of it
Returns the metadata without the bytes

right_distractors: Appends bytes to the end of the object

prompt: This lesson ran the AWS CLI against `moto_server` on a laptop. What can that session show about S3?
hint: What is moto an imitation of?

choices.text: How long a `GET` takes from São Paulo
choices.why: moto answers from the laptop's memory, so its timing says nothing about S3's.

choices.text: The requests and answers of the interface
choices.why: Right. It imitates the HTTP interface, and that is all it speaks for.

choices.text: How many copies of each object S3 keeps
choices.why: moto keeps one copy in memory; S3's replication is not something it imitates.

choices.text: What the requests would have cost
choices.why: Prices come from the price sheet; moto bills nothing and knows no prices.

prompt: `aws s3 ls s3://ana-uploads` printed two `PRE` lines and no objects, though the bucket held two objects. Why?
hint: Where did the listing cut each key?

choices.text: Each key has a `/`, and the listing cut it there
choices.why: Right. Cut at the first slash, both keys became prefixes and none stood alone.

choices.text: The two uploads had not finished when the listing ran
choices.why: Both uploads had finished, and a read after a write sees the object.

choices.text: Only a `--recursive` listing ever shows the objects themselves
choices.why: A key with no slash would appear in the plain listing too, as `index.html` does in the figure.

choices.text: The folders `photos/` and `reports/` were never created
choices.why: Nothing has to exist at a prefix; the uploads worked without any folder.

prompt: Put in order the requests moto logged when `aws s3 mv` renamed `reports/q3.txt`.
hint: Look before copying, and copy before deleting.
items: PUT to the new key, as a copy
trap: Deleting first would leave a moment with no copy at all; the CLI copies first, so for a moment both exist.

prompt: Put the four S3 classes of the sheet in order of storage price in `sa-east-1`, dearest first.
hint: The longer the wait or the fee to read, the cheaper to keep.
trap: The two Glacier lines are close, 0.00830 and 0.00765; Instant Retrieval costs a little more to keep because it can be read at once.

prompt: What does keeping 1,000 GB in Glacier Flexible Retrieval for one month cost in `sa-east-1`, at 0.00765 USD per GB-month?
hint: Gigabytes times price.

prompt: An object is moved to Standard-IA and deleted ten days later. How many days of storage are billed for it in Standard-IA?
hint: The class has a minimum.

choices.text: Ten, the days it was actually there
choices.why: That is how Standard bills. Standard-IA has a minimum stay.

choices.text: Thirty, the class's minimum duration
choices.why: Right. Deleted early, it is billed as though it had stayed 30 days.

choices.text: Ninety, like each class below Standard
choices.why: Ninety is the minimum of the two Glacier classes; Standard-IA's is 30.

choices.text: None: a deleted object is never billed
choices.why: The minimum exists exactly for objects that leave early.

prompt: A lifecycle rule on a whole bucket moves every object to Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days. The bucket also holds the images the company's website shows. What happens to a visitor on day 31?
hint: Can a `GET` read that class directly?

choices.text: The images load in milliseconds, only cheaper
choices.why: That describes Instant Retrieval. Flexible Retrieval needs a restore first.

choices.text: The images load after a few seconds' delay
choices.why: A `GET` does not wait for a restore; it is refused until one has been done.

choices.text: The images are deleted by the rule
choices.why: The rule only moves them; nothing in it expires objects.

choices.text: The images fail to load until each one is restored
choices.why: Right. A `GET` on Flexible Retrieval is refused until a restore, which takes minutes to hours.

prompt: Bucket configuration that moves objects to cheaper classes by age, and deletes them after a set number of days, is called a ___ rule.
hint: It follows an object from creation to deletion.

prompt: Match each protection to what it guarantees.
hint: Two are promises about hardware, two are about requests.

pairs.right: The bytes still exist a year from now
A request for them succeeds right now
An overwritten object can be read as it was
A copy survives the first account's credentials

right_distractors: The object is served faster to distant readers

prompt: S3 Standard is designed for 99.99% availability. A year has 525,600 minutes. How many minutes a year does that design allow requests to fail?
hint: What is 0.01% of the year?

prompt: A cleanup script deletes every key under `invoices/` in an S3 Standard bucket with versioning off. What does eleven nines of durability do for those invoices?
hint: What is durability measured against?

choices.text: Nothing; the store did what it was asked
choices.why: Right. Durability protects what you asked the store to keep, against hardware; a delete is what you asked.

choices.text: They can be recovered from one of the three zones
choices.why: The delete removes the object in every zone; the replicas are not backups.

choices.text: They are kept for 30 days before being removed
choices.why: That is what a lifecycle rule for noncurrent versions does, with versioning on.

choices.text: AWS restores them, since it promises eleven nines
choices.why: Eleven nines is a design figure against lost hardware, not a service that undoes requests.

prompt: In a bucket with versioning on, a `DELETE` names a key and no version. What does the bucket do?
hint: Is anything destroyed?

choices.text: Removes every version of the key
choices.why: Only deleting each version by its id removes it.

choices.text: Removes the current version only
choices.why: Nothing is removed; the current version becomes noncurrent.

choices.text: Adds a delete marker in front of the versions
choices.why: Right. The marker becomes current and the key looks absent, while every version stays.

choices.text: Refuses the request, since versioned keys are protected
choices.why: The request succeeds, which is why the object seems gone.

prompt: Someone deleted `notes.txt` in a versioned bucket, and a listing no longer shows it. How is it brought back?
hint: What is standing in front of the versions?

choices.text: Upload the file again from someone's laptop
choices.why: That writes a new version, if anybody has a copy; the old one was never lost.

choices.text: Turn versioning off so the old version shows
choices.why: Versioning can only be suspended, and that changes nothing already stored.

choices.text: Restore it from Glacier
choices.why: Nothing moved it to Glacier; restore belongs to a storage class, not to deletes.

choices.text: Delete the delete marker by its version id
choices.why: Right. With the marker gone, the last version is current again.

prompt: A 1 GB export is overwritten once a day in a bucket with versioning on and no lifecycle rule. After 30 days of writes, how many GB does the bucket hold for that key?
hint: Every version is kept and billed.

prompt: Match each kind of data to where it belongs.
hint: How does the program reach the data?

pairs.left: PostgreSQL's data directory on one instance
Images many servers and browsers fetch by name
A legacy application that polls a shared directory
Logs kept two years and almost never read

prompt: A news story reports customer records found in an S3 bucket anybody could read. What is the most likely cause?
hint: What state does a new bucket start in?

choices.text: Someone granted read access to everyone
choices.why: Right. The store did what it was told, and somebody told it that everyone could read.

choices.text: Buckets were public by default until 2023
choices.why: Buckets have always been private by default; 2023 added more guards against opening them.

choices.text: Versioning exposed the older copies
choices.why: Versions follow the bucket's access rules; they open nothing by themselves.

choices.text: A zone failed and the data was served unprotected
choices.why: A failed zone makes data unavailable, not public.

prompt: A photo-sharing site runs on four web servers. Users upload pictures, the pages show them, and the team can change the code. Where should the pictures go?
hint: The code can change, so the cheapest shape that fits wins.

choices.text: A `gp3` volume on each server, kept in sync
choices.why: Four copies, four bills, and a synchronisation problem nobody needs.

choices.text: An EFS file share mounted by all four
choices.why: It works, and it is what you choose when the code cannot change; here it can, and objects cost far less.

choices.text: Objects in a bucket, written and read by key
choices.why: Right. Written once, read many times by name, by any server or straight from a browser.

choices.text: Glacier Flexible Retrieval, the cheapest line
choices.why: Every page view would need a restore first; pictures on a page are read constantly.

prompt: In a versioned bucket, the empty version that a `DELETE` adds, which makes the key look absent, is a delete ___.
hint: Remove it and the object is back.

prompt: Which of these does S3 bill even if the bytes stored never change? Choose all that apply.
hint: Storage, requests and history each have a line.

choices.text: The gigabytes stored, per month
choices.why: Yes. The storage line bills every month the bytes are there.

choices.text: Every `LIST` request
choices.why: Yes. `LIST` is priced with `PUT` at 0.00700 per 1,000 in `sa-east-1`.

choices.text: Old versions kept by versioning
choices.why: Yes. Each version is stored and billed like a current object.

choices.text: An empty bucket, for existing
choices.why: No. The bill is for what is stored and what is asked; an empty bucket has neither.
